description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
Output 1: Participants have updated their knowledge about poultry and pig husbandry and entrepreneurship
We were surprised by the lack of knowledge in the basic area of poultry and pig farming. Despite the fact that we found most participants had experience in the sector themselves, it turned out that a lot of knowledge was still missing. We therefore decided that we would still pay a bit more attention to this than originally planned. We did this by splitting the group into two at certain times, so that we could also use our time more efficiently. During our sessions on poultry farming and pig farming, a lot of management questions came up, which we were able to answer (in consultation with the group). Involving the group in particular was important because it also encouraged participants to share knowledge and learn from each other.
Output 2: Participants have developed a new curriculum for poultry and pig husbandry, including training materials and training techniques
As the group of participants consisted mainly of alumni of the university, they were not directly involved in implementation of the university's current curriculum. Therefore, in consultation with our local contacts, we decided that the focus would be more on developing new curricula for newly established training activities. This was carried out in small groups of 2 or 3 participants. So curriculum development did receive full attention, including devising teaching methods and teaching techniques that could be used in the process.
It was originally planned that the development of teaching materials would be from books that participants would receive. These books had also been sent and received (we understood) but on arrival it turned out that only the poultry books had arrived, and not the pig books. This was a setback, but we were able to resolve it by looking up our own material on the internet that could serve as a basis for developing the curricula and teaching materials. An employee of the university is coming to the Netherlands soon and will still bring the missing books (which we ordered extra).
​
Output 3: Participants have access to updated teaching materials on poultry husbandry and poultry processing.
Work was done within the framework of the training to develop teaching materials, but since the basic knowledge on poultry and pig farming was lower than we had expected, we did pay more attention to it. Logical because knowledge has to be there first before it can be transformed into teaching materials for others. Nevertheless, we paid a lot of attention to sharing knowledge with others and which techniques can be used for this purpose. So the participants do have a 'toolbox' with which they can further develop these materials tailored to concrete situations.
​
